title: Multiple-Angle and Composite Equations
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: Multiple-angle and composite trigonometric equations contain expressions such as sin(2x), cos(3x), tan(4x), or other functions of a multiple or transformed angle. The main challenge is not simply solving the trigonometric equation, but making sure that every solution for the transformed angle produces every valid value of x in the required interval. These equations connect the periodic nature of trigonometric functions with algebraic substitution, identities, and systematic solution generation.

content.text: A multiple-angle equation contains an angle such as nx, where n is an integer. Examples include sin(2x) = 1/2, cos(3x) = −1, and tan(4x) = √3.

The key idea is to temporarily treat the entire multiple angle as a single angle. For example, in sin(3x) = 1/2, let θ = 3x. First solve sin(θ) = 1/2, then convert the resulting values of θ into values of x.
Because multiplication changes how quickly the trigonometric function completes its cycles as x changes, multiple-angle equations can have more solutions in a fixed interval than basic equations.

sections.title: General Method for Solving Multiple-Angle Equations

content.text: Step 1: Identify the multiple angle, such as 2x, 3x, or 4x.
Step 2: Introduce a temporary variable if useful. For example, let θ = 3x.
Step 3: Solve the resulting basic trigonometric equation completely using the appropriate general-solution formula.
Step 4: Account for every solution of the multiple angle that lies within the transformed interval.
Step 5: Divide by the coefficient of x only after all relevant solutions for the multiple angle have been generated.
Step 6: Apply the original interval for x and remove any values that fall outside it.
Step 7: Substitute the final answers back into the original equation when necessary.

sections.title: Why Multiple-Angle Equations Have More Solutions

content.text: The basic sine and cosine functions repeat every 2π, while tangent repeats every π. If the input becomes 2x or 3x, that input travels through its normal period more quickly as x increases.

For example, sin(x) completes one full cycle as x moves through an interval of length 2π. sin(2x) completes two cycles over the same x-interval. Therefore an equation involving sin(2x) can intersect a horizontal value multiple times.
This is why simply finding one principal value and dividing by the coefficient can miss valid solutions.

sections.title: Equations of the Form sin(nx) = a

content.text: For sin(nx) = a, solve for the angle θ = nx using the standard sine equation first.
The complete solution for θ is θ = sin⁻¹(a) + 2kπ or θ = π − sin⁻¹(a) + 2kπ, where k ∈ ℤ.
Then replace θ by nx and solve for x. When a restricted interval is given, use the transformed interval to determine which values of k are required.

sections.title: Equations of the Form cos(nx) = a

content.text: For cos(nx) = a, solve the cosine equation for θ = nx first.
The complete solution is θ = ±cos⁻¹(a) + 2kπ, where k ∈ ℤ.
After generating all required θ values, divide by n and retain only the x-values inside the requested interval.

sections.title: Equations of the Form tan(nx) = a

content.text: For tan(nx) = a, solve the tangent equation for θ = nx.
Because tangent has period π, the general solution is θ = tan⁻¹(a) + kπ, where k ∈ ℤ.
After solving for θ, divide by n and apply the original interval for x.
Remember that tangent is undefined whenever cos(nx) = 0, so domain restrictions must be respected.
Double-angle identities are taught in trig-equations-07. Here the focus is their use inside an equation, such as converting sin(2x) or cos(2x) into a solvable form.
Triple-angle identities are part of the identity library in trig-equations-07. Here they are used only when they help solve a multiple-angle equation.
A composite equation may contain a more complicated angle expression such as sin(2x + π/3), cos(3x − π/4), or tan(4x + π/6).
The same principle applies: treat the complete angle expression as a single variable, solve the trigonometric equation, and then solve the resulting algebraic equation for x.
For example, if sin(2x + π/3) = 1/2, let θ = 2x + π/3. Solve sin(θ) = 1/2 first, then solve each resulting linear equation for x.
The coefficient and constant inside the angle must both be handled carefully. Dividing only the trigonometric value or ignoring the constant shift produces incorrect answers.
Some multiple-angle equations cannot be solved conveniently in their current form. A trigonometric identity may be needed first.
For example, cos(2x) = 1/2 can be solved directly, but an equation such as 2sin²(x) − 1 = 0 can be recognized using cos(2x) = 1 − 2sin²(x), giving cos(2x) = 0.
Choose the identity that reduces the equation to a form that can be solved using the basic trigonometric equations.
Do not expand an equation unnecessarily. The goal is to simplify it into a solvable form while preserving the complete set of solutions.
The most important skill in multiple-angle equations is generating every solution in the requested interval.
If x lies in 0 ≤ x < 2π and the equation contains 3x, then 3x lies in 0 ≤ 3x < 6π. The transformed angle therefore covers three full 2π cycles.
This transformed interval explains why an equation involving 3x can have three times as many solutions as the corresponding equation involving x, depending on the equation and boundary conditions.
Never assume that the number of solutions is the same as for the corresponding basic equation. Always examine the interval of the transformed angle.
When an interval is given, transform the interval consistently with the multiple-angle expression and then apply the detailed restricted-interval workflow in trig-equations-09.
After solving the multiple or composite angle, express the complete answer using the general-solution conventions in trig-equations-11.
For multiple-angle equations, substitute the final x-value into the original complete expression. The broader theory of checking and extraneous solutions is in trig-equations-10.
Do not find only the principal value of the multiple angle.
Do not divide by the coefficient of x before generating all relevant solutions for the multiple angle.
Do not forget that the transformed angle has a different interval from x.
Do not use the period of x instead of the period of the transformed angle.
Do not treat tangent as having period 2π. Its fundamental period is π.
Do not ignore domain restrictions when the equation contains tangent, secant, cosecant, or cotangent.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Multiple-Angle General Solution
formulas.expression: sin(nx) = a  ⇒  nx = sin⁻¹(a) + 2kπ  OR  nx = π − sin⁻¹(a) + 2kπ,  k ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Solve the sine equation for the complete angle nx first. Only after generating the required solutions should you divide by n.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Compact Sine General Solution
formulas.expression: sin(nx) = a  ⇒  nx = (−1)ᵏ sin⁻¹(a) + kπ,  k ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: A compact way to represent both families of sine solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Multiple-Angle General Solution
formulas.explanation: Solve the cosine equation for nx first and then divide by n.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Multiple-Angle General Solution
formulas.expression: tan(nx) = a  ⇒  nx = tan⁻¹(a) + kπ,  k ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Tangent repeats every π, so only one family is required. Then solve for x.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Equal Sine Rule
formulas.expression: sin(nx) = sin(θ)  ⇒  nx = θ + 2kπ  OR  nx = π − θ + 2kπ
formulas.explanation: Use the two sine solution families and then solve each equation for x.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Equal Cosine Rule
formulas.explanation: Use both signs to obtain the complete set of cosine solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Equal Tangent Rule
formulas.explanation: Tangent has period π, so solutions differ by integer multiples of π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Double-Angle Identity for Sine
formulas.explanation: Useful when an equation contains a product of sin(x) and cos(x) or when sin(2x) needs to be converted into basic functions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Double-Angle Identity for Cosine
formulas.explanation: Useful for converting between double angles and squared sine/cosine terms.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Double-Angle Form
formulas.explanation: Especially useful when an equation contains cos²(x).

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Double-Angle Form
formulas.explanation: Especially useful when an equation contains sin²(x).

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Double-Angle Identity
formulas.explanation: Useful for equations involving tan(2x), provided the denominator is nonzero and the original tangent expressions are defined.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Triple-Angle Identity
formulas.explanation: Useful for converting equations involving sin(3x) into polynomial equations in sin(x), or vice versa.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Triple-Angle Identity
formulas.explanation: Useful for converting equations involving cos(3x) into polynomial equations in cos(x), or vice versa.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Triple-Angle Identity
formulas.explanation: Useful for equations involving tan(3x), subject to the domain restrictions of tangent.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of sin(nx)
formulas.expression: For n ≠ 0, the fundamental period of sin(nx) is 2π/|n|
formulas.explanation: Explains why increasing the angle coefficient creates more cycles and potentially more solutions over a fixed x-interval.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of cos(nx)
formulas.expression: For n ≠ 0, the fundamental period of cos(nx) is 2π/|n|
formulas.explanation: Useful for understanding the number and spacing of solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of tan(nx)
formulas.expression: For n ≠ 0, the fundamental period of tan(nx) is π/|n|
formulas.explanation: Tangent has fundamental period π, so tan(nx) repeats more frequently as the coefficient n increases.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Zero Sine Equation
formulas.expression: sin(nx) = 0  ⇒  nx = kπ  ⇒  x = kπ/n,  k ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: A frequently used special case. Apply the required interval after solving.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Zero Cosine Equation
formulas.expression: cos(nx) = 0  ⇒  nx = π/2 + kπ  ⇒  x = π/(2n) + kπ/n,  k ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: A frequently used special case for multiple-angle equations.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Zero Tangent Equation
formulas.expression: tan(nx) = 0  ⇒  nx = kπ  ⇒  x = kπ/n,  k ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Tangent is zero at integer multiples of π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Transforming an Interval
formulas.expression: If θ = nx and a ≤ x ≤ b, then for n > 0: na ≤ θ ≤ nb
formulas.explanation: Transform the interval before solving so that every relevant solution for the multiple angle is included.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Pythagorean Double-Angle Relationship
formulas.explanation: Often combined with double-angle identities to convert an equation into a quadratic in sin(x) or cos(x).

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Product-to-Double-Angle Relationship
formulas.explanation: Useful for recognizing products as double-angle expressions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Phase Symmetry
formulas.explanation: Explains the ± form in the general solution for cosine equations.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Supplementary-Angle Relationship
formulas.explanation: Explains why sine equations have two solution families within each 2π cycle.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Periodicity
formulas.explanation: The fundamental periodic relationship used to solve tangent equations.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Composite-Angle Substitution
formulas.expression: If f(ax + b) = c, let θ = ax + b, solve f(θ) = c, then solve ax + b = θ
formulas.explanation: A general strategy for equations containing shifted and scaled angles.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Degree-Radian Conversion
formulas.explanation: Use consistently when a problem mixes degree and radian measures.

examples.question: Solve cos(2x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 2x. Then cos(θ) = 0, so θ = π/2 + kπ. Since 0 ≤ x < 2π, we have 0 ≤ θ < 4π. Therefore θ = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2. Divide by 2: x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4.

examples.question: Solve sin(2x) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 2x. Then 0 ≤ θ < 4π. Since sin(θ) = 1/2, θ = π/6 + 2kπ or θ = 5π/6 + 2kπ. In 0 ≤ θ < 4π, the solutions are π/6, 5π/6, 13π/6, 17π/6. Dividing by 2 gives x = π/12, 5π/12, 13π/12, 17π/12.

examples.question: Solve cos(3x) = −1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 3x. Since cos(θ) = −1, θ = π + 2kπ. The interval becomes 0 ≤ θ < 6π. Therefore θ = π, 3π, 5π. Dividing by 3 gives x = π/3, π, 5π/3.

examples.question: Solve tan(2x) = √3 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 2x. Since tan(θ) = √3, θ = π/3 + kπ. Because 0 ≤ θ < 4π, θ = π/3, 4π/3, 7π/3, 10π/3. Dividing by 2 gives x = π/6, 2π/3, 7π/6, 5π/3.

examples.question: Solve sin(2x + π/3) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 2x + π/3. Then sin(θ) = 1/2, so θ = π/6 + 2kπ or θ = 5π/6 + 2kπ. From the first family: 2x + π/3 = π/6 + 2kπ, giving x = −π/12 + kπ. From the second family: 2x + π/3 = 5π/6 + 2kπ, giving x = π/4 + kπ. Now select values satisfying 0 ≤ x < 2π. The solutions are 11π/12, 23π/12, π/4, and 5π/4.

examples.question: Solve 2sin²(x) − 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Rearrange: 2sin²(x) = 1, so sin²(x) = 1/2. Using cos(2x) = 1 − 2sin²(x), the equation becomes cos(2x) = 0. Therefore 2x = π/2 + kπ. For 0 ≤ x < 2π, we need 0 ≤ 2x < 4π, giving 2x = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2. Hence x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4.

examples.question: Solve 4cos³(x) − 3cos(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Recognize the triple-angle identity 4cos³(x) − 3cos(x) = cos(3x). Therefore cos(3x) = 0. Hence 3x = π/2 + kπ. Since 0 ≤ x < 2π, 0 ≤ 3x < 6π. Thus 3x = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2, 9π/2, 11π/2. Dividing by 3 gives x = π/6, π/2, 5π/6, 7π/6, 3π/2, 11π/6.

examples.question: Solve cos(3x − π/4) = √2/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 3x − π/4. Then cos(θ) = √2/2, so θ = ±π/4 + 2kπ. First: 3x − π/4 = π/4 + 2kπ, giving x = π/6 + 2kπ/3. Second: 3x − π/4 = −π/4 + 2kπ, giving x = 2kπ/3. Generate all values in 0 ≤ x < 2π from both families and remove duplicates. The solutions are 0, π/6, 2π/3, 5π/6, 4π/3, 3π/2.

examples.question: How many solutions does sin(4x) = 0 have for 0 ≤ x < 2π?
examples.solution: sin(4x) = 0 means 4x = kπ. Therefore x = kπ/4. The interval 0 ≤ x < 2π requires 0 ≤ kπ/4 < 2π, so 0 ≤ k < 8. Thus k = 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7, giving 8 solutions.

examples.question: Solve tan(2x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: tan(2x) = 0 when 2x = kπ. Hence x = kπ/2. In 0 ≤ x < 2π, k = 0,1,2,3, giving x = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2. These values are valid because tangent is defined at each corresponding angle.

examples.question: Solve sin(3x) = 1 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
examples.solution: Let θ = 3x. Then 0° ≤ θ ≤ 1080°. Since sin(θ) = 1, θ = 90° + 360°k. Within the transformed interval, θ = 90°, 450°, 810°. Therefore x = 30°, 150°, 270°.

key_ideas: Treat the complete multiple angle such as nx as a single angle while solving the trigonometric equation.
Solve the multiple angle completely before dividing by its coefficient.
Transform the interval for x into an interval for nx so that no solutions are missed.
Multiple-angle functions complete their cycles faster, so they can produce more solutions over the same x-interval.
Use the correct general solution for sine, cosine, or tangent.
Tangent has period π, whereas sine and cosine have period 2π.
Composite angles such as ax + b must be handled as a complete expression.
Use double-angle and triple-angle identities when they transform an equation into a more convenient solvable form.
Always return to the original interval after solving.
Check final answers in the original equation when transformations could introduce or lose solutions.
For general solutions, keep the integer parameter k ∈ ℤ.
The coefficient multiplying x affects the number and spacing of solutions.
The most important practical skill is systematic solution generation rather than finding only a principal angle.
misconceptions: Finding only the principal value of nx and assuming it is the only solution.
Dividing by n before generating all solutions for nx.
Using the interval for x directly when solving for nx.
Assuming sin(nx) and cos(nx) have period 2π in x. Their x-period is 2π/|n|.
Assuming tan(nx) has period 2π in x. Its x-period is π/|n|.
Forgetting the second solution family for sine.
Using the sine or cosine general solution for tangent.
Ignoring a constant shift inside a composite angle such as 2x + π/3.
Dividing only part of an equation such as ax + b = θ incorrectly.
Using a multiple-angle identity without checking the original domain.
Assuming every algebraic root obtained after an identity transformation is automatically valid.
Counting solutions without checking whether the interval includes its endpoints.
Assuming that more complicated-looking equations always require identities; sometimes direct substitution into the multiple angle is simpler.
Stopping after obtaining a general solution without listing restricted-interval solutions when the problem asks for them.
